qs.q: A patient's cervical biopsy reveals high-grade dysplasia driven by human papillomavirus. What molecular event serves as the primary oncogenic driver?
o: Episomal viral DNA replication driving high levels of structural L1 capsids
Translocation of cellular myc oncogenes adjacent to viral enhancer sequences
Methylation of upstream regulatory regions silencing viral transcription entirely
Mutation of host tumor suppressor genes via targeted viral transposase action
Genomic viral integration leading to upregulated E6 and E7 oncoprotein expression
qs.e: Integration of high-risk HPV DNA into host chromosomes disrupts E2, causing overexpression of E6 and E7 oncoproteins that degrade p53 and Rb.

qs.q: A 65-year-old man undergoes resection of a firm sigmoid colon mass. Which microscopic finding distinguishes this invasive adenocarcinoma from severe epithelial dysplasia?
o: Complete absence of goblet cells in affected crypts
Loss of nuclear polarity with hyperchromatic stratification
Marked increase in mitoses in crypt epithelium
Tumor glands penetrating the muscularis mucosae
Disruption of the basement membrane beneath surface crypts
qs.e: Invasive adenocarcinoma is definitively diagnosed by tumor cells crossing the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa.

qs.q: A 50-year-old woman with a history of long-standing ulcerative colitis undergoes surveillance colonoscopy. Random biopsies reveal high-grade dysplasia within flat mucosa. Which genetic alteration is typically an early, initiating event in this pathway?
o: A. Inactivating mutations of the adenomatous polyposis coli gene
B. Amplification of the MYC proto-oncogene on chromosome 8
C. Inactivation of the TP53 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17
D. Activation of the KRAS oncogene through codon 12 mutations
E. Loss of SMAD4 tumor suppressor function on chromosome 18
qs.e: APC gene inactivation is an early initiating event in both sporadic colorectal carcinogenesis and colitis-associated neoplastic pathways.

o: A. Proton pump inhibitor therapy use
qs.e: Fundic gland polyps are frequently associated with long-term use of proton pump inhibitors, causing parietal cell protrusion and cyst formation.

Zero percent because the mother is unaffected.

qs.q: A 42-year-old man with a 12-year history of extensive ulcerative colitis is scheduled for long-term malignancy surveillance. Which specialized endoscopic technique is recommended during his colonoscopy to detect dysplasia?
qs.e: Chromoendoscopy is specifically recommended during surveillance colonoscopy for dysplasia in patients with long-standing extensive colitis. Capsule endoscopy is primarily used for small bowel Crohn's disease and is not the standard for colonic dysplasia surveillance.

qs.q: A 68-year-old man presents with fatigue and macrocytic anemia. Bone marrow examination reveals hypercellularity and dysplasia limited strictly to the erythroid lineage. Which specific classification category applies?
qs.e: Refractory anemia (RA) is characterized by dysplasia in red blood cells only. RCMD involves dysplasia in two or more myeloid lineages.

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with unexplained cytopenias undergoes a bone marrow biopsy and peripheral blood smear review. Which leukocyte abnormality is most characteristic of myeloid dysplasia in this patient?
o: Auer rods located strictly in lymphocytes
qs.e: Hyposegmented nuclei with bilobed forms (Pelger-Huët anomaly) is a classic finding of dysgranulopoiesis in myelodysplastic syndrome. Hypersegmented neutrophils are more typical of megaloblastic anemias caused by vitamin deficiencies.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Dysplasia refers to abnormal cellular development, often characterized by disordered growth and maturation. It is a precancerous condition, indicating an increased risk of progression to invasive carcinoma. Early detection and management are crucial to prevent malignant transformation.

sections.p: Dysplasia is a pathological term describing abnormal cellular proliferation and maturation, characterized by architectural disorganization and cytological atypia. It represents a spectrum of changes that fall short of malignancy but indicate an increased risk of developing cancer. Diagnosis is made histologically by examining tissue biopsies.
b: Architectural disorganization: Loss of normal tissue arrangement.
Cytological atypia: Variations in cell size and shape (pleomorphism), nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia (darker nuclei), and increased mitotic activity.
Often found in epithelial tissues, such as the cervix, skin, and gastrointestinal tract.

sections.p: Dysplasia is typically graded based on the extent of epithelial involvement, which helps predict the likelihood of progression to invasive carcinoma. This grading system guides clinical management decisions.
b: Mild dysplasia (Low-grade): Atypical changes confined to the lower third of the epithelium.
Moderate dysplasia: Atypical changes extending into the middle third of the epithelium.
Severe dysplasia (High-grade): Atypical changes involving more than two-thirds of the epithelium, approaching carcinoma in situ (CIS).
Carcinoma in situ (CIS): Full-thickness involvement of the epithelium by atypical cells, but without invasion through the basement membrane.

sections.p: Dysplasia arises from chronic irritation, inflammation, or exposure to carcinogens that induce genetic mutations and abnormal cell growth. The specific causes vary depending on the tissue involved.
b: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection: A primary cause of cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal dysplasia (e.g., subtypes 16 and 18).
Chronic inflammation: Conditions like Barrett's esophagus (from chronic GERD) or inflammatory bowel disease.
Chemical carcinogens: Tobacco smoke (oral, lung, bladder dysplasia), alcohol (oral, esophageal dysplasia).
Ultraviolet (UV) radiation: A major cause of skin dysplasia (actinic keratosis).
Genetic predisposition: Some inherited syndromes increase the risk of dysplasia in specific organs.

sections.p: Dysplasia often presents asymptomatically, especially in its early stages. It is frequently discovered during routine screening examinations or investigations for other conditions. When symptoms do occur, they are usually non-specific.
b: Cervical dysplasia: Usually asymptomatic, detected by Pap smear.
Oral dysplasia (leukoplakia, erythroplakia): White or red patches in the mouth, often painless.
Skin dysplasia (actinic keratosis): Rough, scaly patches on sun-exposed skin.
Gastrointestinal dysplasia: May be asymptomatic or present with symptoms related to the underlying condition (e.g., reflux, bleeding).

sections.p: The primary investigation for suspected dysplasia is a biopsy, followed by histological examination. The choice of biopsy technique depends on the location of the suspected lesion.

t.a: Biopsy (e.g., colposcopy-directed biopsy for cervix, endoscopy with biopsy for GI tract, punch biopsy for skin)
t.b: Answers: Is dysplasia present, and if so, what is its grade? Result: Histological confirmation of architectural disorganization and cytological atypia, graded as mild, moderate, or severe.

Answers: Are there abnormal cells in the cervix that warrant further investigation? Result: Atypical Squamous Cells of Undetermined Significance (ASCUS), Low-grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (LSIL), or High-grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL) indicate the need for colposcopy and biopsy. Answers: Is high-risk HPV present, which increases the risk of cervical dysplasia? Result: Positive for high-risk HPV subtypes (e.g., 16, 18) indicates increased risk and may guide management, especially for low-grade lesions.

sections.p: The most significant complication of dysplasia is its potential to progress to invasive carcinoma. Certain features or locations carry a higher risk of malignant transformation.
b: High-grade dysplasia: Carries a significantly higher risk of progression to invasive cancer.
Erythroplakia: Red lesions are more likely to already show severe dysplasia or early invasive carcinoma compared to white lesions (leukoplakia).
Persistent dysplasia: Dysplasia that does not resolve after initial management or recurs.
Dysplasia in specific sites: Such as the transition zone of the cervix, which is a common site for high-risk HPV-related changes.

sections.p: Management of dysplasia aims to remove or destroy the abnormal cells to prevent progression to invasive cancer. The approach depends on the site, grade, and patient factors.
b: Observation: For mild dysplasia, especially in younger patients, as it may regress spontaneously. Regular follow-up is essential.

Excisional procedures: Surgical removal of the dysplastic tissue (e.g., Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure (LEEP) or cold knife conization for cervical dysplasia). This allows for complete histological assessment.
Ablative procedures: Destruction of dysplastic tissue (e.g., cryotherapy, laser ablation for cervical dysplasia). These are less suitable if a full histological specimen is needed.
Treatment of underlying causes: Such as HPV vaccination to prevent new infections, or management of chronic reflux in Barrett's esophagus.

sections.p: Regular follow-up is critical to monitor for recurrence or progression of dysplasia. Prevention strategies focus on reducing exposure to risk factors and early detection.
b: Regular surveillance: Repeat Pap smears, colposcopy, or endoscopy as per clinical guidelines, depending on the site and grade of dysplasia.
HPV vaccination: Highly effective in preventing HPV-related cervical and other anogenital dysplasias.
Lifestyle modifications: Avoiding tobacco and excessive alcohol, practicing safe sex, and sun protection.
Screening programs: Organized screening (e.g., cervical cancer screening) for early detection.

sections.p: It is important to differentiate dysplasia from other conditions that may appear similar but have different clinical implications.
b: Hyperplasia: An increase in the number of cells, but with normal maturation and architecture. Not necessarily precancerous.

Metaplasia: Reversible change of one mature cell type into another mature cell type in response to stress (e.g., squamous metaplasia in the bronchus). Not inherently dysplastic, but can precede dysplasia.
Condyloma (genital warts): Caused by HPV, but typically not considered premalignant, though the same risk factors apply and high-risk HPV types can co-exist and cause dysplasia.
Inflammation: Can cause reactive cellular changes that mimic mild dysplasia, but these changes resolve once the inflammation subsides.

sections.p: Several factors can lead to misinterpretation of dysplasia results, potentially affecting patient management.
b: Sampling error: A biopsy may miss the most severe area of dysplasia, leading to an underestimation of its grade.
Inflammation: Reactive cellular changes due to inflammation can be mistaken for mild dysplasia, leading to unnecessary interventions.
Observer variability: Interpretation of histological slides can vary between pathologists, especially for mild dysplasia.
Inadequate specimen: A biopsy that is too small or poorly preserved may not allow for an accurate diagnosis.

faq.q: What is the difference between dysplasia and cancer?
faq.a: Dysplasia is a precancerous condition where cells show abnormal growth but have not invaded surrounding tissues. Cancer (carcinoma) involves invasion through the basement membrane into underlying tissues.

faq.q: Can dysplasia go away on its own?
faq.a: Mild dysplasia, particularly in the cervix, can sometimes regress spontaneously, especially in younger individuals. Moderate to severe dysplasia is less likely to regress and usually requires intervention.

faq.q: How long does it take for dysplasia to turn into cancer?
faq.a: The progression from dysplasia to invasive carcinoma is usually a slow process, often taking a decade or more. This provides a window for diagnosis and conservative treatment.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect focused history and perform a systematic exam to identify dysplasia‑related signs and rule out mimics.
b: History: age, sex, ethnicity; sexual history and contraceptive use; smoking, alcohol, occupational exposures; chronic infections (HPV, TB); inflammatory bowel disease duration; family history of cancers; symptoms: pain, bleeding, dysphagia, weight loss.

Examination: inspect cervix for lesions, palpate for cervical motion tenderness; oral cavity for leukoplakia/erythroplakia; skin for actinic keratosis; abdomen for masses or organomegaly; rectal exam for mucosal changes; note any ulceration or induration.

t.b: Detects surface lesions; positive if erythema, ulceration, or plaques present, suggesting dysplasia but not specific.
Positive indicates possible cervical inflammation but not dysplasia; helps differentiate from PID.
Hard, indurated plaques suggest malignant transformation; soft lesions may be benign.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a tiered approach: cytology, imaging, and histology, with clear interpretation criteria and contingency plans when tests are limited.
b: Colposcopy with acetic acid – visualizes acetowhite epithelium; positive if mosaic or punctate patterns.
Biopsy – gold standard; grading per WHO 2019 criteria: mild, moderate, severe, CIS.
Endoscopic surveillance (chromoscopy, NBI) – identifies dysplastic lesions in IBD.
Immunohistochemistry (p16INK4a) – supports HPV‑related dysplasia.

t.b: Answers: is there cervical dysplasia? Positive if HSIL/CIN3; high risk of progression (30‑50% over 10‑20 years).
Answers: is the lesion likely high‑grade? Positive if mosaic/punctate acetowhite pattern; indicates need for biopsy.
Answers: severity? Mild (≤1/3 epithelium), moderate (1/3‑2/3), severe (>2/3), CIS (full thickness).
Answers: dysplasia in IBD? Positive if nodular or depressed lesions; guides targeted biopsies.
Answers: HPV‑driven dysplasia? Positive staining supports high‑grade lesion.

sections.p: Apply WHO 2019 classification and organ‑specific staging to guide management.
b: Cervical: CIN1 (mild), CIN2 (moderate), CIN3 (severe/CIS).
Oral: mild, moderate, severe dysplasia; CIS defined by full‑thickness atypia.
Skin: actinic keratosis (low‑grade), Bowen’s disease (CIS).

t.b: Defines dysplasia grades based on epithelial thickness involvement; used across organs.
≥1 cm dysplastic lesion in UC; high risk of progression; often requires colectomy.

sections.p: Differentiate dysplasia from benign or inflammatory mimics using key distinguishing features.
b: Reactive epithelial hyperplasia – uniform nuclei, no pleomorphism; no atypia.
Inflammatory pseudotumour – infiltrates with inflammatory cells, no atypia.
HPV‑negative lesions – may mimic dysplasia but lack p16 positivity.

t.b: Points: uniform cells, no nuclear atypia; separate by lack of pleomorphism.
Points: dense inflammatory infiltrate, no atypia; separate by histology.

sections.p: Treat dysplasia according to grade, site and patient factors, using a clear escalation ladder.
b: 1. Confirm diagnosis with biopsy and histology.
4. Post‑treatment surveillance: repeat cytology or endoscopy at 6 months, then annually for 3 years.
5. Escalate to specialist referral if incomplete excision, recurrence, or invasive disease suspected.

t.b: High‑grade lesions may be managed conservatively if patient is unfit for surgery, but close monitoring is essential.
Topical 5‑fluorouracil or imiquimod for superficial skin dysplasia; avoid in pregnancy.
Prevents recurrence in cervical dysplasia; not therapeutic.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: When using topical or systemic agents for dysplasia, monitor for local and systemic toxicity.
b: Topical 5‑FU: skin irritation, ulceration; treat with emollients, discontinue if severe.
Imiquimod: local inflammation, flu‑like symptoms; advise rest, stop if severe.
Systemic retinoids: mucocutaneous dryness, hepatotoxicity; monitor liver enzymes.
Topical steroids: skin atrophy, secondary infection; use sparingly.

t.b: Retinoids + antacids can reduce absorption; counsel patient to take separately.
If hepatotoxicity occurs with retinoids, stop drug and repeat LFTs.
All systemic retinoids are teratogenic; use contraception.

sections.p: Progression to invasive carcinoma or systemic spread requires urgent action.
b: 1. New ulceration, bleeding, or rapid growth in a dysplastic lesion—immediate re‑biopsy.
2. Persistent high‑grade dysplasia after treatment—refer to oncology or surgical specialist.
3. Development of pain or functional impairment—evaluate for invasion.
4. Systemic signs (fever, weight loss) in patients with known dysplasia—rule out metastasis.

t.b: Any change in lesion morphology or patient symptoms warrants re‑evaluation.
Refer within 2 weeks of suspected invasion or recurrence.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities alter presentation, diagnosis and treatment of dysplasia.
b: HIV: increases risk of high‑grade cervical dysplasia; use more frequent screening.
TB: may mimic dysplastic lesions on imaging; obtain microbiology before treatment.
Malnutrition: impairs wound healing post‑excision; optimise diet.
Pregnancy: avoid systemic retinoids; use cryotherapy or LEEP if necessary.
Diabetes: increases infection risk; monitor glucose.
Herbal remedies: some contain carcinogens; inquire about use.
Alcohol: exacerbates liver toxicity with retinoids; counsel abstinence.
Renal/liver failure: adjust drug choice; avoid hepatotoxic agents.

t.b: Elderly may have reduced regenerative capacity; consider less aggressive surgery.
Use cryotherapy or LEEP where excisional devices are unavailable; rely on visual inspection with acetic acid.

sections.p: Tailor dysplasia management to children, pregnancy, elderly, HIV, and resource constraints.
b: Children: use non‑invasive screening; avoid systemic retinoids; refer to pediatric oncology if invasive.
Pregnancy: prefer LEEP or cryotherapy; postpone systemic therapy until postpartum.
Elderly: balance surgical risk with benefit; consider watchful waiting for low‑grade lesions.
HIV: intensified screening intervals; consider antiretroviral status when choosing systemic agents.
Low‑resource settings: rely on visual inspection with acetic acid, cryotherapy, or LEEP; use generic 5‑FU for skin dysplasia.

t.b: Ensure viral suppression before elective surgery to reduce infection risk.
Avoid high‑dose systemic retinoids; use lowest effective dose.

facts: High‑grade dysplasia (HGD) in ulcerative colitis covering ≥1 cm is a dysplasia‑associated lesion or mass (DALM) and warrants colectomy or endoscopic resection.
CIN 3 (HSIL) progresses to invasive cervical cancer in ~30‑50 % over 10‑20 years if untreated.
Severe dysplasia involves >2/3 of epithelial thickness; carcinoma in situ involves full thickness without invasion.
Barrett’s esophagus dysplasia risk: low‑grade dysplasia 0.5‑1 %/year, high‑grade 5‑10 %/year for progression to cancer.
In oral leukoplakia, dysplasia risk: low‑grade 1‑2 %/year, high‑grade 10‑15 %/year.
Colorectal dysplasia in ulcerative colitis: low‑grade 0.5‑1 %/year, high‑grade 5‑10 %/year.
Cytological atypia: nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, increased N/C ratio.
Histological grading: mild (lower third), moderate (middle third), severe (upper two thirds).

vivas.q: What histological features define high‑grade cervical dysplasia (CIN 3)?
vivas.a: Full‑thickness epithelial atypia with loss of maturation, nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, increased mitoses, but no stromal invasion.

vivas.q: A 35‑year‑old woman has HSIL on Pap smear. What is the next step?
vivas.a: Colposcopic directed biopsy of the most abnormal area; if CIN 3 confirmed, refer for LEEP or conization.

vivas.q: Why is a 1 cm dysplastic lesion in ulcerative colitis called a DALM?
vivas.a: DALM stands for dysplasia‑associated lesion or mass; it indicates a large, high‑grade area that usually requires surgical intervention.

vivas.q: Which endoscopic technique is recommended for dysplasia surveillance in long‑standing ulcerative colitis?
vivas.a: Chromoscopy or virtual chromoendoscopy (NBI) to enhance mucosal patterns and identify dysplasia.

vivas.q: What is the risk of progression from CIN 3 to invasive cancer if left untreated?
A 65‑year‑old man has a firm sigmoid mass. Which microscopic finding distinguishes invasive adenocarcinoma from severe dysplasia?
vivas.a: Invasive adenocarcinoma shows stromal invasion with desmoplasia; severe dysplasia remains confined to epithelium.

vivas.q: A 68‑year‑old man has macrocytic anemia and erythroid‑line dysplasia. Which classification applies?
vivas.a: Refractory anemia with ring sideroblasts (RARS) if ring sideroblasts ≥20 %; otherwise, myelodysplastic syndrome, erythroid type.

vivas.q: Which leukocyte abnormality is most characteristic of myeloid dysplasia?
vivas.a: Atypical neutrophils with pseudo‑lobulation (pseudo‑segmentation) and hypogranulation.

vivas.q: During a newborn exam, which maneuvers check for hip dysplasia?
vivas.a: Barlow and Ortolani tests: gentle adduction/abduction and posterior pressure to detect dislocation or subluxation.

vivas.q: An infant with congenital renal dysplasia has hyponatremia and dilute urine. What explains this?
vivas.a: Under‑developed collecting ducts impair concentrating ability, leading to dilute urine and sodium loss.

vivas.q: A 38‑year‑old woman has renal artery stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia. How do the ischemic kidney arterioles appear?
vivas.a: They show a string‑of‑beads pattern with alternating stenosis and aneurysmal dilatation.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for oral dysplasia?
mcqs.e: High‑fat diet is not a recognized risk factor.

mcqs.q: A Pap smear shows ASC‑US. What is the recommended next step?
mcqs.e: HPV DNA testing stratifies risk for ASC‑US.

mcqs.q: Which histological feature distinguishes carcinoma in situ from invasive carcinoma?
mcqs.e: Invasion of stroma defines invasive carcinoma.

cases.v: A 42‑year‑old man with 12‑year history of ulcerative colitis presents for surveillance colonoscopy. Endoscopy shows a 1.2 cm flat lesion with irregular vascular pattern.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Dysplasia‑associated lesion or mass (DALM) – high‑grade dysplasia.
Endoscopic mucosal resection or surgical colectomy depending on extent and patient factors.

qs.q: Which surveillance interval is appropriate after resection?
qs.a: Repeat colonoscopy in 3–6 months to ensure complete removal and monitor for recurrence.

mistakes: Assuming HSIL always requires immediate LEEP; it may be managed with colposcopic biopsy first.
Overestimating progression risk of CIN 3 as >70 %; correct is 30‑50 % over 10‑20 years.
Confusing severe dysplasia with carcinoma in situ; the latter involves full‑thickness epithelium without invasion.
Treating a 1 cm ulcerative colitis dysplasia as low‑grade; it is a DALM and usually needs resection.
Ignoring the need for chromoscopy in ulcerative colitis surveillance.
Misidentifying pseudo‑segmentation as normal neutrophil morphology in myelodysplasia.
Assuming all dysplastic lesions are malignant; many are low‑grade and can be monitored.
